12500.d:
ARTERIA editions are created by autonomous agents which are drawing paths following a set of rules.

Artéria means artery in Old Occitan, a Romance language spoken in the south of France.  

Agents have a default behavior: they go straight ahead, have children, die when they meet the trajectory of another agent... 
The system starts with dozens of random initial parameters: recursion level, agents position and size, colors, birth angle and distribution... The possibilities are endless.
 Finally, some local rules can be applied (ex: all the agents in the upper half rotate slowly).
The output is the result of the initial parameters, interactions between agents and local rules.  

ARTERIA is the most complex and varied series I have created so far.
My goal was to experiment playing with an algorithm that can generate a huge variety then tame and modulate it with local rules. In other words, control the chaos enough to create meaning and emotion.

I wrote an article about the project: https://immutablecollective.art/writing/arteria-making-of/

12504.d:
In 1946 the artist M.C. Escher created the mezzotint ‘Eye’, a rendering of his own eye as reflected in an extremely convex mirror. Although he liked the technique, the process of creating each mezzotint was slow, and as a result he only created eight mezzotints over the course of his career.

The image is striking: a highly-detailed rendering of the human eye, complete with reflections, and there, at the centre of the eye, is a skull: a reminder that “we are all confronted with death whether we like it or not”, and a fulfilment of what Escher saw as a need to portray an observer reflected in the convex mirror of the eye.

I decided to recreate ‘Eye’ generatively, my intention being to produce an infinite range of pieces based on Escher's painstakingly-constructed original. The iris, pupil, skull and eyelid are generated using random processes, shaped with the aid of probabilities and limited colour palettes. Layers are built up over a sequence of three hundred and sixty frames. and the skull is formed from a cloud of shaped, random points in the centre of the pupil.

Sizes, colour palettes and striations are all chosen from the initial hash value, and there are a number of rare features to be discovered.

Interactivity is enabled once the piece is clicked on, and layers can be activated or deactivated using the number keys. Press 'I' for more information.

For my first drop on the new fxhash v1.0 I wanted to make something different. So I challenged myself to write a raymarcher like the ones I use in my shaders but in p5.js and make a fully procedural scene with it. It's a bit tricky to work with vectors once you are used to GLSL, but I managed to write a decent algorithm that scans a grid and slowly draws the image. It draws it with circles and triangles for the grass. The first thing I used for testing was a SDF of a plane with some tall bars on it. Then I was trying different distortions on the shapes and in one moment the results gave me the idea of a scene with mushrooms and grass on an undulated terrain. Later I added a small river and a cloudy sky. I think I was inadvertently inspired by some children's books I had when I was a kid.

A Gabriel Graph is a special kind of graph in graph theory where an edge can only be formed between two nodes if the circle formed by those two nodes contains no other nodes in the graph.  A Random Geometric Graph is a graph where an edge can only be formed between two nodes if they are less than a certain distance away from each other.  In this project, I have created random Gabriel Graphs and Random Geometric Graphs, where the graphs have a random number of nodes and each node has a random position.  Each node is assigned a color, and each edge is colored according to the two nodes at each end, with a gradient line and a gradient circle which slowly transitions from one color to the other.  Users can interact with the project to remove the nodes, edge lines, or edge circles, choosing how they would like the graph to be displayed.

Made with p5.js

Press 'a' to toggle the edge circles on and off.
Press 's' to toggle the edge lines on and off.
Press 'd' to toggle the nodes on and off.

12641.d:
Pages (of the mind) is an original work that captures the flavor of Abstract Art painting from the mid-1960's era. It is based on an algorithm that creates three dimensional cylinders made up of planes or pages. Imagine creating an object by opening a book such that the front covered is rotated around its spine to touch the back cover. The pages create a cylindrical space. Many paper party favors are created this way.

Initially an array of "centers" are created for a number of cylinders to be some what uniformly distributed on a white background in a grid pattern. Then many random variables are employed. Each cylinder is given a random length and diameter. From their initial center positions each cylinder is slightly translated and rotated from a normal position to a unique spatial orientation. Then each cylinder is drawn in perspective to produce an interesting distortion. 

Color and varying page opacity is what makes this piece. No gradients are used. A random color is assigned to each cylinder. The vibrant color comes from applying transparency to the rendering of each of the overlapping pages that comprise the object. The more the pages overlap the more saturated the color of the cylinder becomes, more so nearer to its central axis.

By special request, 10% of the time, the wireframes that define the cylinders are drawn to show their three dimensional structure. If you don't care for this feature simply generate another.

Description of Seasons of Siskiyou Series

Surrounding my home, covering more than one million acres, is the Rogue River - Siskiyou National Forest which takes up three southern Oregon counties and one northern California county.  It’s a magical place that fills the imagination and lifts the spirit; a place that inspires with its uniqueness, its legends, and its larger-than-life vistas.

Each season in the Siskiyous is a unique experience unto itself.  So, with an attention to the feelings this place evokes at any given time of the year, I designed four generative tokens to create an impression of the emotion–the calming quietness; the peaceful solitude; the overwhelming contrasts and variety of forms, shapes and textures; the magic and playful mystery; the welcomingness and foreboding.  These four works feature clever and inventive creative coding techniques in a rich, graphic style to craft a stunning impression of the Seasons of Siskiyou.


Token 4 of 4 - The Weight of Winter (1990 x 1080) p5js Generative Token.

All good things must come to an end.  After a glorious time of renewal and rebirth, the months of growth and bounty come to a close.  A time of reflection and rest approaches.  All that can be done has been done; and, all one can do is endure the season of slumber.

As light fades with the shyness of the sun, the need to sleep takes over as the creatures of the wilderness test their preparedness.  Travelers to warner lands have offered farewell to those brave enough to stand against the coming snows.  Those who have remained will carry the weight of winter.  The festival of fall had provided so much to carry them through to the colors of spring.  Has it been enough?

The weight of winter can be crushing; but, it’s the pressure that shapes the designs of persistence, endurance and perseverance required to fight against it.  With its paler of indifference, the monochrome landscape of winter hides the brilliance of those schemes aimed at mastering the challenges of survival.  With their perfect adaptations, nature survives to take on winter’s heft with defiant joyfulness and triumphant serenity.  

The Weight of Winter features a generative atmosphere with distant mountains; flow-field conifer trees on noise-wave foothills; a random cluster of subject conifers in the mid-space; and a flow-field tree branch with an interpolated dusting of snow.  Diamond dust – small spears of ice – are simulated with an optical-effect along with random snowflakes.  A generative ‘conspiracy’ of ravens are scattered along the tree tops.

The preparations for the first mission began in 2142. It had become clear that mining petroleum on Earth would soon become financially unfeasible, so looking to other planets was the only logical choice. It took seventeen more years to perfect the technology so that the first colonists could reach Proxima b within the lifetime of one generation.

After 45 years of travelling at almost one-tenth of the speed of light, they reached their new home. It was rich in petrochemicals but scarce in the nutrients necessary for long term human survival. After merely six generations, humanity was forced to travel once again in search of a new world. The four missions that parted from the Proxima system to colonise other possibly habitable planets in the galaxy sparked a new age of human civilisation that would never see itself united and thriving again.

Eventually, all the colonies became independent societies as their differing interests drove them apart. Each small civilisation chose its path, wandering the void of space alone. The beauty of generative art is that the process is fully recorded. Art is not created through a 'magic hand', but rather a systematic formula that is reproducible. Although variability and randomness can be introduced, it is controlled and contained. The visibility of the process also sheds light to things that might not be visible in the final image outcome.

For example, in 'Hidden Message', a message is written behind the layer of threads. Although not visible, this can be verified as a fact by looking at the source code. This allows the creator to play with what is visible to the viewer and what's not, opening a new realm of artistic possibilities.
